doc.title: Hentoff Nat — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

chapter: Civil liberties, family and the press
title: Jazz as the Constitution in action and black musicians' Americanism
summary: Citing Max Roach, he says black musicians, despite Jim Crow, were more invested in what America should be.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Politics, race and the state of the country

blocks.x: When you mentioned Constitutional couch potatoes, then I go back to your friends Rex Stewart and the people in the Ellington band – let’s say all – to make a general – all black people, but especially the African-Americans of your generation that you knew, to whom the Constitution, I guess, was not some abstract thing, or the real manifestations of it on a day-to-day level, I guess that so many . . .
white folks – so many others were just kind of blind to, and on a day-to-day level they . . .

That’s why, when you think about it, somebody like Max Roach was the first person I ever heard who said jazz was like the Constitution in action: individuals getting together and being more than their individual selves. Yeah, these guys were so much more involved in – despite the pervasive Jim Crow at the time, they were more involved
in what this country was supposed to be. They had hassles being themselves. That made them even stronger as people and through their music.
